title: A Leader's Guide to Waiting Well
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short piece argues that leaders mismanage waiting by reflexively filling every idle moment with email or scrolling, treating unoccupied time as pure waste. Drawing on David Maister's classic psychology-of-queues research, it notes that a wait's felt length depends on whether it's occupied, explained, and certain, not on the clock. Its actual advice is counterintuitive: leaders should sometimes deliberately let a wait be boring, because research on boredom suggests idle, unstructured attention is exactly when the brain does its best associative, creative work. The mechanism it proposes is to load an open, unresolved problem into mind right before the wait begins, then let it sit passively rather than actively working it — the same mental state behind 'shower thoughts.' It positions this as a genuinely productive use of dead time, distinct from and superior to filling the gap with more email.
points: Distress during a wait tracks how it's perceived (occupied vs. unoccupied, explained vs. unexplained, certain vs. uncertain), not the actual clock time.
Filling every idle moment with email or a quick task trades away the brain's best creative-thinking conditions for the illusion of being productive.
The technique isn't just 'don't check your phone' — it requires deliberately loading an unresolved problem into mind right before a wait begins.
Unfinished tasks stay active in memory and keep nagging until resolved, so a leader entering any prolonged wait likely already has several open loops running unconsciously.
Insight comes from holding a question loosely and letting the mind wander around it without direct effort — the same mechanism behind ideas that surface on a walk or in the shower.
quotes: David Maister's classic analysis of the psychology of waiting lines makes the case that distress in a queue has less to do with the clock than with how the wait is perceived.
But research on boredom and the brain's neural system suggests that idle, unstructured time is when the mind does some of its best creative work.
The counterintuitive idea is to occasionally let a wait be boring on purpose and to treat the discomfort as a signal that the mind is ready for the challenge of thinking privately.

An unfinished task stays active in memory long after a completed one has been forgotten, nagging at the mind until the loop is closed. A leader going into a prolonged wait has several of these open loops running whether they know it or not.
Instead of active analysis, the best creative ideas come from holding the question loosely and allowing the mind to wander around it without direction, the way it wanders during a shower or walk.

Leaders who can sit in a line, a layover, or in silence without reflexively filling it or resenting it, and who let the mind wander instead, are often rewarded with ideas and solutions they couldn't generate any other way.
